36.title: The king who argued
36.hook: a king claims he gives life and death, so Ibrahim asks him to bring the sun from the west (2:258)
36.carry: the sun rises where it rises
36.howItsDone: Muslims read 2:258 as a model of clear, calm reasoning, and teachers often point to Ibrahim's move to the sun as a way to leave a twisted debate without anger.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire made cool, bardan wa salaman. Your line was cool and safe. Today, Ibrahim faces a king.
screen: `THE FIRE MADE COOL — COOL AND SAFE.`

segments.voice: You've been in this argument. A family dinner, a comment thread at midnight. The other person isn't really listening. Every point you make, they twist, and somehow you're three steps from where you started, defending something you never said. You could keep going all night. Some people do. Today Ibrahim stands before the most powerful man in his world, a king, in an argument about God. And the king is very good at twisting. Watch what Ibrahim does.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT AT MIDNIGHT.` → `EVERY POINT, TWISTED.` → `IBRAHIM BEFORE A KING.`

segments.voice: Surah two, verse two fifty-eight. Think of the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord, because God had given him a kingdom. Power went to his head. The Qur'an doesn't name him; tradition calls him Namrud, Nimrod. Ibrahim says, in Pickthall's words: “My Lord is He Who giveth life and causeth death.” The king answers: “I give life and cause death.” The commentators tell how he proved it: two condemned prisoners brought in, one executed, one pardoned. There. Life and death. It's a trick. That isn't what Ibrahim meant at all. He could have spent the afternoon explaining the difference. He doesn't. He moves to something no trick can reach. Paraphrasing the verse: God brings the sun up from the east, “so do thou cause it to come up from the West.” And then: “Thus was the disbeliever abashed.” The Arabic word, buhita, means stunned, struck dumb. Ibrahim doesn't win by being louder, or by untangling every twist. He steps out of a rigged argument and points at the sky. The sun rises where it rises. It doesn't need Ibrahim to win the debate to keep rising. And the story stops right there. No victory lap, no punishment, no speech. The king is silenced, and the story moves on. That's the lesson under the lesson: some arguments aren't worth winning point by point. You can say one true thing, simply, and let the sun do the rest.

segments.voice: There's probably an argument you're still having, out loud or in your head, the one you rehearse in the shower; hear the twist, your comeback, and theirs. Now picture a sunrise, slow, ordinary, unbothered, coming up exactly where it always does, and notice how small the argument gets beside it: you don't have to win it. If you pray, you can hand it to the One who brings up the sun.

37.title: The friend of Allah
37.hook: Ibrahim is called the friend of Allah for his wholehearted trust (4:125)
37.howItsDone: Muslims call Ibrahim Khalilullah, the friend of God, and many talk to God in their own words in du'a, the personal prayer that can be made any time, in any language.

segments.voice: Yesterday: buhita, the king struck dumb by the sun from the west. Your line was the sun rises where it rises. Today, the name Ibrahim is known by.
screen: `BUHITA — THE SUN RISES WHERE IT RISES.`

segments.voice: There are the people you know, and then there are one or two friends. Not the ones you follow, or work with. The one you could call from a hospital waiting room. With that friend there's no performing. You can say the plain thing: I'm scared. I don't know what to do. And they listen. Ibrahim has watched the stars, broken the idols, faced a crowd, a fire and a king. Kings have titles. Prophets have titles too. But one name the Qur'an gives Ibrahim, the one Muslims still call him by, is the name for that kind of friend.
screen: `PEOPLE YOU KNOW, AND A FRIEND.` → `THE ONE YOU'D CALL FROM ANYWHERE.` → `IBRAHIM'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Surah four, verse one twenty-five. In Pickthall's words: “Allah (Himself) chose Abraham for friend.” The Arabic word is khalil, stronger than the everyday word for a friend. Some scholars trace it to the root kh-l-l, which has to do with the gaps between things, what passes through. Scholars explain khulla as a closeness that goes all the way through, a love that fills every space in the heart and leaves no room for anything else. So when Ibrahim, watching the star set, said I love not things that set, he was clearing that space. Muslims still call him Khalilullah, the friend of God. The city of Hebron, where tradition places his tomb, is called al-Khalil in Arabic to this day. Jews and Christians know him by the same title, friend of God, in their scriptures too. What does that friendship sound like? In surah twenty-six, Ibrahim talks about God not like a subject to a king, but like someone describing the person closest to him. Paraphrasing: He created me, and He guides me. He feeds me and gives me to drink. Then, in Pickthall's words: “And when I sicken, then He healeth me.” Food, water, getting sick. The most ordinary parts of a day. That's how a friend talks. And friendship goes both ways. Ibrahim trusted wholeheartedly: on the day of the fire, the report says, his words were simply: God is enough for us. A khalil doesn't hold back half of himself. He says the plain thing, and he listens.

segments.voice: If you pray, spend a minute talking to God like a friend, no formal words, just what today was like, what worries you, what you're glad of, the way Ibrahim talked about food and water and getting sick. Then spend the rest of the time listening, in the quiet. If you don't pray, say those same plain things in your mind to the friend you could call from anywhere, and then listen.

38.title: Guests with news
38.hook: angels visit Ibrahim, he hurries to feed them, and his wife laughs at the news of a son
38.howItsDone: Welcoming guests with food and drink is a familiar part of Muslim home life, and teachers often cite the hadith about honoring the guest as the reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalil, the friend of Allah, the name Ibrahim carries. Your line was a friend listens.

The doorbell rings, and nobody was expected. A quick inventory starts: anything in the fridge? Laundry on the couch? Ibrahim, peace be upon him, gets that doorbell. Strangers arrive at his tent. They say peace, and he says peace back. He doesn't know who they are. He doesn't ask what they want. The Qur'an says he slipped away to his household, quietly, and came back with a whole roasted calf. Not a snack. A feast, for people he'd never met. Then something strange happens. The guests don't eat. Their hands don't reach for the food.
screen: `STRANGERS AT THE TENT.` → `A WHOLE ROASTED CALF.` → `THEIR HANDS DON'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells this story twice, in Surah Hud and in Surah adh-Dhariyat, and each telling adds a detail. Surah Hud says he did not delay. Adh-Dhariyat says he went to his family quietly, so the guests wouldn't feel like a burden, brought a fat calf and set it close to them. Then, gently: won't you eat? That's hospitality in two verses: hurry, don't make a fuss, put the best you have within reach. The Qur'an calls them the honored guests of Ibrahim, and the honor starts with the host. They don't eat, and Ibrahim feels a flicker of fear. Commentators explain that in his world, a guest who refused your food might mean you harm. They say, don't be afraid. They're messengers, angels, sent on to the people of Lut, with news for this house. His wife is standing nearby. The Qur'an doesn't name her; Muslim tradition knows her as Sarah. She laughs. How can I bear a child, an old woman, with a husband this old? The angels answer: are you amazed at the command of Allah? A son is coming, Ishaq, and after him a grandson, Ya'qub. Commentators don't agree why she laughed: the surprise, relief, the sheer impossibility. The text leaves it open. Jews and Christians tell this visit too, at the oaks of Mamre in Genesis. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made the host's side part of faith: a hadith in Bukhari says whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let them honor their guest. Ibrahim fed strangers before he knew they carried good news. The feeding came first.

39.title: Hajar in the valley
39.hook: Ibrahim leaves Hajar and baby Isma'il in a dry valley, and she asks: did Allah command this? then we will not be lost
39.carry: then we will not be lost
39.howItsDone: Muslims remember Hajar at Mecca, where the valley she was left in became the city around the Ka'ba; her trust is often retold in sermons on tawakkul, reliance on Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dayf, the honored guests fed before anyone knew their news. Your line was hurry to the guest. Today, a valley with nothing in it.

A valley with nothing in it. No trees, no well, no town. Rock on both sides, heat coming up off the ground. A man walks in with a woman and a baby, sets down a leather bag of dates and a skin of water, and turns to go. She gets up and follows him. Ibrahim, are you leaving us here, in a valley with no people and nothing in it? He doesn't answer. She asks again. He keeps walking, and he doesn't look back. What she asks next is short, and it isn't an accusation.
screen: `A VALLEY WITH NOTHING IN IT.` → `SHE FOLLOWS HIM.` → `HE DOESN'T LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: This story isn't told in the Qur'an itself. It comes from a long hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated from Ibn Abbas. Hajar is the mother of Ibrahim's son Isma'il; Jews and Christians know her as Hagar, from Genesis. She follows Ibrahim, asking, and he won't answer. So she changes the question. Did Allah command you to do this? He says yes. And she says, in effect: then He will not let us be lost. And she walks back to her baby. She didn't stop asking. She found the one question that mattered, got her answer, and let it hold her. That's not the same as feeling fine. The dates and water are about to run out, and tomorrow we'll see what that costs her. But her trust is the ground she stands on while she runs. Then the hadith gives us Ibrahim's side. When he reached a place where they couldn't see him, he turned toward the valley, raised his hands and prayed. That prayer is in the Qur'an, in Surah Ibrahim: our Lord, I have settled some of my children in a valley without crops, near Your sacred House, so that they may establish prayer. So make the hearts of people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may give thanks. He didn't look back at them. But out of sight, he looked back at the valley, and asked for everything they'd need. That empty valley is Mecca. Pilgrims now walk where she stood.

If you pray, you can hand it over by name.

40.title: Seven runs and a spring
40.hook: Hajar runs seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, and water springs by the baby's feet
40.howItsDone: During Hajj and Umrah, pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, a rite called sa'y, and drink Zamzam water, which pilgrims often carry home to share with family and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hajar in the valley, asking the one question that mattered. Your line was then we will not be lost. Today, the water runs out.

To the door and back. To the door and back. A parent pacing a hallway at three in the morning, because moving is the only thing left to do. That's where we find Hajar. The dates are gone. The water skin is empty. She is thirsty, the baby is thirsty, and Isma'il is crying and twisting on the ground. She can't bear to watch. So she climbs the nearest hill and looks for anyone at all. Nobody. She runs down, across the valley floor, and up the hill on the other side. Nobody.
screen: `THE WATER SKIN IS EMPTY.` → `SHE CLIMBS AND LOOKS.` → `NOBODY.`

segments.voice: The same hadith in Bukhari tells it. The first hill is Safa, the second is Marwa. She goes back and forth between them seven times, climbing, looking, running the low stretch between. On the seventh, she hears a voice. She says: you've made me hear you; if you can help, help. And there, by the baby, is an angel, striking the ground with his heel, and water comes up out of the dry earth. She hurries to hold it in, scooping sand around it into a little basin, filling her skin. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, telling this story long afterward, adds a line of pure tenderness: may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il. If she had left it alone, Zamzam would have been a flowing stream. That spring still flows in Mecca, in the grounds of the great mosque, where pilgrims drink from it and carry it home in bottles for the people who couldn't come. Where the name comes from, nobody knows for certain. A story people tell says Hajar called out zam, zam, hold still, gather, as she held the water in. Take that as a story, not a record. And the running didn't stop with her. The Prophet said that's why people go between the two hills. Pilgrims at Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwa seven times, and in one marked stretch the walk quickens, as hers did. The Qur'an calls Safa and Marwa among the signs of Allah. So a rite of the pilgrimage retraces a mother's search: not her calm, her running. It honors the searching as much as the finding.

segments.voice: If there's room where you are, stand and take seven steps one way, then seven back, seven times, slowly; if you can't stand, trace it with a finger on your knee. With each length, think of one thing you're still looking for, still hoping for, still running toward. If you pray, make a small prayer on each length; if not, just count, and feel your feet.

41.title: The dream
41.hook: Ibrahim dreams he must sacrifice his son, the son says do as you're told, and Allah ransoms him with a great sacrifice
41.howItsDone: At Eid al-Adha, during the days of Hajj, many Muslim families sacrifice a sheep, goat or cow in memory of Ibrahim's ransom and share the meat among the household, relatives and friends, and people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zamzam, water from dry ground after seven runs. Your line was keep running; the water comes. Today's story is the hardest one in Ibrahim's life.

The baby from the valley has grown. The Qur'an says he's old enough now to walk alongside his father, to work with him, the age when a son starts to be company. And Ibrahim has a dream. In it, he is sacrificing his son. Some stories are too heavy to hold lightly, and this is one of them. For a prophet, a dream like that isn't just a dream. What would you do with it? Ibrahim does something surprising. Before anything else, he tells his son, and asks him what he thinks.
screen: `OLD ENOUGH TO WALK WITH HIM.` → `A DREAM TOO HEAVY TO HOLD.` → `HE ASKS HIS SON.`

segments.voice: It's in Surah as-Saffat. Ibrahim says: my son, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so look, what do you think? A father asking. The son answers: my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient. Then comes one of the most careful verses in the Qur'an. When they had both submitted, and he had laid him down on his forehead. Both submitted. The Arabic is aslama, the same root as islam and Muslim: to surrender, to hand yourself over. Father and son, together. And at that moment, a call: O Ibrahim, you have already fulfilled the dream. This was the clear test. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. The knife never falls. What was asked for was the willingness, and it was given. Which son? The Qur'an doesn't name him here. Most Muslim scholars say Isma'il, partly because the good news of Ishaq comes a few verses later, as if he hadn't been born yet. Some early Muslim scholars said Ishaq. Jewish and Christian scripture tell the story of Abraham and Isaac. Each tradition holds its own reading. Every year at Eid al-Adha, the festival of sacrifice, Muslims around the world remember this moment. Many families sacrifice an animal and share the meat in thirds: for the household, for friends and relatives, and for people in need. The ransom became a meal. And a story about a knife becomes, once a year, a story about feeding people.

Hold it in mind, say quietly, not today, and notice the little pull in you that resists; that pull is what the story is about. If you pray, you can offer the small thing up.
The dream. A father who asked, a son who agreed, and a ransom that meant the knife never fell.
Your line: the test was the willingness. Saying no to the small thing is the whole of it. Day forty-one, done.

42.title: Raising the House
42.hook: Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the foundations of the House, praying, accept this from us
42.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for each of the five daily prayers, a direction called the qibla; pilgrims on Hajj and Umrah walk around it seven times and pray near the Station of Ibrahim.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dream, and a ransom before the knife fell. Your line was the test was the willingness. Today, the end of the week, and the last day with Ibrahim.

If you've ever built something with your father, or your kid, you know it's never really about the shelf. One holds the board, one drives the screw, someone drops the level, somebody laughs. The thing gets built, and something else gets built too. Back to the empty valley. There's a spring there now, and people have come to live around it. Ibrahim comes back, and Isma'il is a grown man, sharpening arrows by the water. Ibrahim says, Allah has commanded me to build a House here. Will you help me? And his son says yes.
screen: `BUILDING WITH YOUR FATHER.` → `THE VALLEY HAS A SPRING NOW.` → `WILL YOU HELP ME?`

segments.voice: The Ka'ba is a plain, cube-shaped stone building in the center of the great mosque in Mecca, draped in black cloth. The Qur'an tells believers, wherever they are, to turn their faces toward it in prayer. That direction is called the qibla. A Muslim in Chicago or Jakarta faces this way on a prayer rug. Surah al-Baqarah gives us the building site. Ibrahim and Isma'il are raising the foundations of the House, and as they work, they pray: our Lord, accept this from us. You are the Hearer, the Knower. Not look what we built, not remember our names: they ask only that the work be received. In the hadith in Bukhari, Isma'il carries the stones and Ibrahim sets them, and when the wall grows too high, Ibrahim stands on a stone to keep building. That stone is still there, near the Ka'ba, called the Station of Ibrahim, and the Qur'an says to take the place where Ibrahim stood as a place of prayer. Some traditions say the House was first founded long before Ibrahim, even by Adam, and that Ibrahim raised it again. The Qur'an says he raised its foundations. And this week's stories meet here: the valley where Hajar asked her question, the spring where she ran, the son who said do what you are commanded. Ibrahim started these eleven days looking at a star, a moon, a sun, and loving what doesn't set. He ends them facing one House.
screen: `A CUBE OF STONE — AND THE QIBLA.` · `OUR LORD, ACCEPT THIS FROM US.` · `THE STATION OF IBRAHIM.` · `THE WEEK MEETS IN ONE PLACE.` · then, large: `KA'BA.`

segments.voice: Build something small your hands can finish in a minute, stack three books, fold a napkin, line up the pens on your desk, make your bed properly, and go slowly, putting the whole of yourself into one small job. If you pray, you can say, as they did, our Lord, accept this from us. If not, notice what it feels like to make something without needing anyone to see it.
Ka'ba. The cube-shaped House in Mecca that Ibrahim and Isma'il raised, and that Muslims face in every prayer.
Your line: accept it from us. Eleven days with Ibrahim: the stars, the idols, the fire, the guests, the valley, the spring, the dream, the House. Six weeks in.
